ageRange: Pediatric trauma, all ages — the compensated-shock physiology point applies most dramatically in younger children with more robust compensatory reserve
purpose: What's specifically different about pediatric trauma resuscitation: a child's ability to mask significant blood loss with a normal blood pressure until very late, and the weight-based blood product/TXA dosing that follows from using weight rather than fixed adult doses.

body.text: Compensated shock — the single most important pediatric-specific point

A child can lose a substantial fraction of circulating blood volume while MAINTAINING a normal blood pressure — pediatric physiology compensates via tachycardia and vasoconstriction far more effectively and for far longer than an adult's, right up until it suddenly can't. By the time hypotension appears, the child has already lost significant volume and decompensation can be abrupt and severe. Do NOT wait for a falling blood pressure to recognize and treat shock in a pediatric trauma patient.

items: Early/subtle signs of significant blood loss in a child: tachycardia (often the earliest and most sensitive sign — but also nonspecific, since pain/fear cause it too), narrowing pulse pressure, delayed capillary refill, cool/mottled extremities, and a change in mental status (irritability progressing to lethargy) — a normal-appearing blood pressure does not exclude any of this.
Treat the CLINICAL picture (tachycardia, poor perfusion, mechanism) as your primary signal, using blood pressure as a late-stage confirmatory finding rather than the trigger to start resuscitating.
Once decompensation starts in a child, it can progress rapidly — the same compensatory reserve that masked the early blood loss leaves little margin once it's exhausted.
Initial PRBC bolus: 10 mL/kg (a rough weight-based analog to the adult 1-unit-at-a-time approach), reassessed after each aliquot rather than committing to a large fixed volume upfront.

For ongoing/massive hemorrhage: balanced ratio transfusion (PRBC:plasma:platelets, conceptually mirroring the adult 1:1:1 massive transfusion approach) scaled by weight — many centers use weight-zone-based 'packs' (see pedi-tape-weight-zones) bundling pre-calculated volumes to avoid real-time math under pressure.

Avoid over-reliance on crystalloid in a child with significant hemorrhage — the same balanced-blood-product-forward philosophy as adult hemorrhagic shock management applies; large-volume crystalloid resuscitation dilutes clotting factors and doesn't carry oxygen.

body.text:
DOSE: loading dose 15 mg/kg IV (maximum 1 g) over roughly 10-20 minutes, followed by a maintenance infusion of 2 mg/kg/h for at least 8 hours or until bleeding has stopped.

EVIDENCE: registry and combat-trauma data support a mortality benefit in severely injured, significantly hemorrhaging children, similar in direction to the adult CRASH-2 evidence base, though the pediatric trial evidence base is smaller.

TIMING: as in adults, earlier administration (within the first few hours of injury) is the generally accepted principle — don't delay TXA while sorting out other resuscitation priorities in a child who clearly needs it.
Everything else follows the standard primary-survey framework

Airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure — the sequence and priorities are the same as adult trauma (see trauma-primary-survey).

Pediatric-specific anatomic/physiologic adjustments are already covered elsewhere in this app:
- airway anatomy differences — see peds-difficult-airway
- weight-based drug/fluid dosing generally — see pedi-tape-weight-zones and the weight-zone-tagged drug cards

This module intentionally covers only the two points above (compensated shock, and weight-based blood/TXA dosing) that are both genuinely distinct AND not already addressed by those other modules.
